Testimony of Maine Health Care Association and Maine Hospital Association
Before the Committee on Health and Human Services ln Support of LD 1769, An Act to Ensure Data Reporting for Temporary Nurse Agencies
Friday, May 2, 2025

Senator lngwersen and Representative Meyer as well as Distinguished Members of the Health and Human Services Committee:

My name is Ben Hawkins, and I serve as the Director of Public Affairs for the Maine Health Care Association. We represent approximately 200 nursing homes, assisted living centers, and
residential care facilities across the state. Our mission is to empower members to ensure the
integrity, quality, and sustainability of longterm care in Maine.

On behalf of the Maine Health Care Association and our colleagues at the Maine Hospital
Association, l am pleased to testify in support of LD 1769, An Act to Ensure Data Reporting for
Temporary Nurse Agencies. This legislation would require the Department of Health and
Human Services to provide an annual report to the joint standing committee of the Legislature havingjurisdiction over health and human services matters summarizing the annual reports
submitted by temporary nurse agencies.
LD 1769 builds upon prior legislation, LD 451 that passed in the 131" Legislature, which requires Temporary Nurse Agencies (TNAs) to register annually with the Department of Health and Human Services and to report data on temporary staffing on a yearly basis. This data includes a number of important metrics such as the total number of employees placed in health care
settings in Maine, average duration, state of licensure for those employees, total and average
amounts charged to the health care facility each quarter, and total and average wages pi to
the employee each quarter, as well as total and average stipends paid to the employee each

quarter. The original legislation (LD 451) required the Department to make a report of TNA data
to this Committee. This bill makes that report on an on-going requirement for the Department to compile this data and present a report to this committee each year.
Long term care facilities and hospitals across Maine are struggling. They are struggling to keep their doors open and meet the needs of their communities because of the ongoing staffing crisis and a lack of adequate and timely reimbursement. Reliance on temporary agency staffing increased significantly during the pandemic and is still not back to pre-pandemic levels. For example, Maine's nursing homes utilization of temporary agency staffing increased from a
statewide average of 22% in 2022 to 26% in 2023 (graph on page 3). The new nursing facility rate model has a built-in assumption that usage of temporary staffing will reduce to 10% by January 2026, which we sadly don't anticipate happening. Consequently, nursing home
MaineCare rates will decrease by $12.85 per MaineCare resident per day starting 1/1/26. The decreased MaineCare rates will put additional strain on providers.
The Maine Hospital Association reports that agency staffing has decreased some over the last
few years, but it is still very costly:
0 FY 23 - $450M 0 FY 24 - $375M 0 FY 25 (projected) - $320M
Policymakers need to have accurate and up-to-date information to inform decision-making. The impact of temporary nurse agencies on the labor market cannot be entirely estimated by individual providers or associations. Having the Division of Licensure and Certification collect this important data on an annual basis will help to identify trends over time.
Now that we have one year's worth of baseline data, it is important to keep collecting this
information. We urge the committee to vote ought to pass on LD 1769. Thank you for your time.

Testimony of the Division of Licensing and Certification
Maine Department of Health and Human Services
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services
Neither for nor against LD 1769, An Act to Ensure Data Reporting for Temporary Nurse Agencies
Sponsor: Senator Baldacci
Hearing Date: May 2, 2025
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services, my name is Bill Montejo, and I serve as the Director of the Division of Licensing and Certification (DLC) in the Maine Department of Health and Human Services. I am here today to testify neither for nor against LD 1769, An Act to Ensure Data Reporting for Temporary Nurse Agencies.
This bill requires the Department of Health and Human Services to provide an annual report to the joint standing committee of the Legislature having jurisdiction over health and human services matters summarizing
the annual reports submitted by temporary nurse agencies.
The Division of Licensing brought to the Legislature's attention that the language in 22 MRS �2131 did not
require an annual report, which is something the previous Legislature expressed interest in. The Division was previously prepared and is willing to provide this report annually.
Additionally, the Division is pleased to offer a few amendments for the Committee's consideration in order to
strengthen the oversight of Temporary Nurse Agencies in Maine should the bill pass. First, we would ask the
Committee to consider expanding the statutory definition of a Temporary Nurse Agency to explicitly include all relevant business models that are subject to registration. The Division has concerns about entities that consider themselves a staffing marketplace, and not a temporary nursing agency. These entities suggest they are only a
conduit and not an employer -- however, this creates a barrier to the required background check process. We can
provide more context if needed. Second, we suggest clarifying that verification of Certified Nursing Assistants (CNA) eligibility through Maine Background Check Center is required even when the agency is indirectly
involved in employment arrangements. Third, that penalties collected, not registrations fees, which go to the
General Fund, be directed into a dedicated account to fund Temporary Nurse Agency oversight as we are seeing
a greater use of the attorney general's office.
I want to reiterate that the Division is prepared and is willing to provide this report amiually as the language
currently states.
Thank you for your time and attention. I would be happy to answer any questions you may have and to make
myself available for questions at the work session.

Testimony of Glen Cyr 5/2/2025
LD 1769, An Act to Ensure Data Reporting for Temporary Nurse Agencies Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and Honorable Members of the Committee on Health and Human Services.
My name is Glen Cyr and I am the Senior Vice President of Finance for North Country Associates, Inc which oversees over 20 long term health care facilities throughout Maine. I am testifying today on behalf of LD 1769 and in favor to the bill as proposed. I reported 2 years ago to this committee on the exploding 3rd party nursing labor costs going from $5 million to $10 million to $25 million and eventually $40 million annually for the organizations which I work with. It is common knowledge that many health care facilities have closed as a result of these spiraling costs. I have been involved with several facility closures or sales of facilities which were repurposed to other uses. It was not an enjoyable experience. The state and

legislature did step in a provide temporarily financial assistance and we appreciated that. Thank you.
Our industry as a whole were collectively paying over $150 million dollars annually for long term care 3rd party nursing agency services from the Maine Health Care Association (MHCA)survey data from 2021 thru 2022.
I do not have any current data for the overall long term care industry, but our organization's temporary nursing costs stand at approx. $27 million annually for all facilities for 2024 and that includes a facility which closed and was spending approx. $10+ million on its own.
The overall trending of agency costs is beginning to slowly reduce but not as quickly as we may all want it to and part of this may be attributable to less bed capacity.
Hospitals in Maine were paying even much more during this time period (figures which may have exceeded $500 million in the same time period) and continue to pay and now the sad trend of hospital closures is underway.
Do you see a pattern here?
I want to be very clear in this statement - I am not here to take funding away from the hard working and dedicated nursing caregivers in Maine. They are the backbone and life blood of providing care to our residents, but many nurses have become independent contractors thru this 3rd party nursing care model and companies are profiting from it in record numbers both

locally and nationally. Of the estimated 240+ registered 3rd party nursing agency companies, only a handful are from Maine. Most of from out of state and are focused on the maximize financial return they can achieve.
There are countless articles and reports of this business model through the United States. Care is now being incentivized by money to a whole new level.
Maine care is the biggest payor for care in Maine and makes up over 70+% of our funding and as Stuarts of our tax dollars by both the Legislature and DHHS, shouldn't you know what agencies are charging, spending and profiting from us all.
The continue collecting of vital and important data is critical so you can view for yourselves and the fiscal impact of this industry to health care and the taxpayers of Maine.
Thank you for your time and serving and representing Maine.

Good morning Senator lngwersen, Representative Meyer, and esteemed members of the Joint Standing
Committee on Health and Human Services. My name is Joe Baldacci, and l represent Senate District 9, which includes Bangor and Hermon. I am pleased today to introduce LD 1769, "An Act to Ensure Data
Reporting for Temporary Nurse Agencies."
This bill builds upon previous legislation that l sponsored (LD 451 from the 131" Legislature), which
required temporary nurse agencies to register annually with the DHHS/Division of Licensing and Certification. The legislation also required these temporary staffing agencies to submit data to the Department, including the total number of employees placed in health care settings in Maine, average duration, state of licensure for those employees, total and average amounts charged each quarter to the health care facility, total and average wages paid to the employee each quarter, total and average stipends paid to the employee each quarter, etc.
The original bill had a report date of no later than December 6, 2023 for DHHS to report to the HHS Committee. It was interpreted as a single report. This bill, LD 1769, would make that annual report to the HHS Committee an ongoing requirement.
Lawmakers need to make policy decisions based upon facts and data so this ongoing reporting requirement will help ensure accurate and up-to-date data is available. As you know, long term care
facilities continue to face serious staffing challenges. Workforce levels are the lowest the sector has
seen in over a decade. We estimate we lost between 10 and 15% of caregivers during the pandemic, and
temporary agency staffing continues to be high in long term care, and across other health care sectors
as well.
I thank you all for your time and consideration.

Introduction
The Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), through the Division of Licensing and Certification (DLC), regulates Temporary Nurse Agencies (Agencies or TNAs) in the State of Maine. Public Law 2023, Chapter 434, An Act to Ensure Transparent and Accountable
Temporary Nurse Agencies, enacted 22 MRSA �2l 31 which enhanced DLC's oversight of
TNAs. This includes ensuring employee quality assurance, prohibiting predatory recruitment practices by TNAs, and a requirement on agencies to submit an annual report to Department of
Health and Hmnan Services.
Prior to the revisions to 22 MRSA �213l, DLC's interaction with TNAs consisted of answering
questions in relation to registrations, reviewing applications, and issuing registration letters and
maintaining files for each registered TNA.
The changes in law, which became effective on October 25, 2023, provide more oversight of
TNAs by DLC, outlines TNAs responsibilities, and provides a new definition of a TNA as . . " .a
business entity or subdivision of a business entity that primarily provides nurses, certified nursing assistants and other qualified staff to another organization on a temporary basis within this State."
Due to the timing of the general effective date for the First Special Session of the 131*`
Legislature, the authority and staff person granted by this section and legislation were not effective soon enough to complete a fill report of the required information by the deadline in
December 2023. As such, this report aims to provide baseline information about the TNAs
operating in Maine ahead of a complete report next year.
In order to provide the Legislature and stakeholders with a baseline set of data on TNAs, DLC
conducted a voluntary survey of TNAs in November 2023. The survey was sent to all registered TNAs on November 7, 2023. The deadline for submitting responses was November 19, 2023,
and the deadline was extended to November 26, 2023, as the response rate was lower than
desired upon the first deadline. Of the 287 registered TNAs in Maine, all were solicited and 66
participated, reflecting a 23 percent response rate.
The survey addressed critical areas such as types of employees placed in healthcare settings,

employees placed by licensure/certification category, and average duration of employee

placements. It also shed light on financial aspects such as rates TNAs charged facilities per

employee category, wages paid to employees per category, and stipends paid to employees per

category. Furthermore, it assessed licensing status, training/education compliance, and

background checks of placed employees, all crucial for maintaining quality and compliance in healthcare staffing in
